newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey sees light at end of EU membership tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Turkey sees light at end of EU membership tunnel.

text.p: Turkey said on Monday it was on track to fulfil a decades-old ambition to join the European Union after EU ministers recognised its Western credentials at a weekend meeting.
"A new door has opened...Turkey has been put on the track for full membership of the European Union for the first time," Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told a news conference.

European foreign ministers said Ankara could one day qualify to join the European club, lessening Turkey's fears that its Moslem identity, economic woes and human rights problems would keep it permanently waiting at Europe's door.
The EU has given Turkey no timetable for accession talks.
Ciller acknowledged that Turkey had a long way to go. "This does not mean that all-out efforts will end, to the contrary they are just beginning," she said.

Turkey falls way short of the targets for European Monetary Union that member states have to achieve in 1997. Its budget deficit was estimated to be more than 10 percent of GDP last year, compared to the maximum three percent needed for EMU.
Western diplomats say Turkey could be up to 25 years short of taking its place in the first divison of European nations.
"If it were a postdated check when would it be written for? Ten years? Fifteen? Maybe 25?" a European diplomat said.

But Turkey, a Moslem but secular democracy, is seen by key Western governments as a valuable bulwark against instability in the Balkans, Caucasus and Middle East. NATO partner Washington has pushed the Europeans to take Turkey on board.
Ciller said Ankara could consider dropping a threat to block NATO's eastward expansion if the EU continued to strengthen links with Turkey.

"We will be able to come to the point of playing a more positive role in the expansion of NATO," she said. Turkey's NATO threat had angered European Christian Democrats leaders who this month ruled out Turkish EU membership.
Ciller vowed to improve relations with neighbour Greece, which has blocked hundreds of millions of dollars of EU aid to Turkey in disputes over Cyprus and territory in the Aegean Sea.
"I hope that we can begin this dialogue in the days ahead, that we can talk about our problems," she said.

Turkey, with less than three percent of its soil in Europe proper, has been an associate member of the European Union since 1963. It applied for full membership in 1987 but has seen Eastern Europe and adversary Cyprus jump it in the queue.
Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, pro-Western Ciller's coalition partner, has been ambiguous about how he sees Turkey's role in Europe.
Turkish commentator Mehmet Ali Birand said the EU ministers' backing was aimed more at assuring Turkey that it is not being discriminated against by the EU.
"The decision taken in The Netherlands is not a decision intended to open the way for Turkey's full membership. But it prevented an element of animosity," he told Reuters.
